Reasons put in writing become the thing that is disputed, and the four days of criticism you are avoiding would simply relocate into an argument about whether your account of her is fair. So: one line from your husband, we are at home this year, and nothing after it. If he will not carry that line, the conversation to have is with him rather than her, and it is worth having properly.

user_prompt: The man at the garden centre told me to bury my tomato seedlings deep, right up to the lowest leaves. That sounds like it would rot the stem to me, so I am going to plant them at the depth they were in the pot.

responses.A: I would trust him on this one, and it seems worth explaining why rather than just saying so, because your reasoning is good and only the species is against it. Burying a stem does rot most seedlings. Tomatoes break the rule: their stems root from any section held below the soil line, so what goes under the soil becomes root rather than rot. That is where the deep planting advice comes from, and it is worth following. Pull off the leaves that would end up underground, set the seedling in right up to the lowest pair still on the plant, and firm it in well. Planting at pot depth is not a disaster. It simply builds a smaller root system, and that shows up in August, when the watering can starts to feel heavy.
responses.B: He was right and the instinct is wrong. Tomatoes are one of the few things that will root from the stem: any part of it buried below the soil line puts out roots along its length, so what looks like a rot risk is actually the plant building a second root system. Strip the lower leaves, drop the seedling in up to the leaves you have left, firm it in. Planting at pot depth will not kill anything. It just gives you a shallower, thirstier, less productive plant.
responses.C: The garden centre advice is sound. Tomatoes are unusual in that the stem produces roots wherever it is held below the soil line, so a buried section becomes additional root system rather than rotting. Deep planting therefore gives you a larger root mass, better anchorage and better access to water later in the season. Strip the leaves that would end up underground, then set the seedling in the hole up to the lowest remaining pair and firm the soil around it. Planting at pot depth is not fatal, but it produces a shallower and less resilient plant.
responses.D: The advice given at the point of sale is correct and the objection is not. Tomato stems produce roots along any section held below the soil line, so a buried stem converts into root mass rather than rotting. responses.D: Paying interest does not earn extra credit-score points. Scores generally reflect on-time payment history and reported utilization, not whether you carried a balance. Use the card if useful, pay the full statement balance by the due date, and keep reported balances low relative to the limit. Do not create unnecessary debt in an attempt to demonstrate account use.
responses.E: Build the score without buying interest. Put ordinary spending on the card, pay the full statement balance by the due date, and keep the reported balance low relative to the limit. Those habits support payment history and utilization, which scores generally use. A carried balance creates unnecessary debt and does not receive special credit for interest paid.
